newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Coffee soars to 2-1/2 year high, oil and cattle fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Coffee soars to 2-1/2 year high, oil and cattle fall.

text.p: Coffee prices soared to a 2-1/2 year high on Wednesday as worries returned about the amount of available supplies for roasters this year.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery closed at 208.05 cents a pound, up 15.65 cents or eight percent for the day and the highest price for coffee since September 1994.

Sparking the rally was a monthly report issued by the Green Coffee Association of New York after the market closed on Tuesday showing supplies of green coffee stowed in U.S. warehouses rose in March by only 111,000 132-pound bags to a total 1,657,000 bags.

Most analysts had forecast a rise of between 250,000 and 300,000 bags, with some looking for a build-up of supplies of as much as 700,000 bags due to stepped-up shipments from Latin America in recent weeks to cash in on higher prices.

"A lot of people expected it to be higher," said Stephen Smith, the president of South Futures, a brokerage firm in Miami. "There were a lot of coffee shipments recently and that's what eveyone was watching."
Smith said one reason the warehouse stocks were lower than expected was that roasters caught short of coffee over the winter have been taking delivery direct at plants.

"Roasters have been building stocks and have a lot of finished products," Smith said. "They got caught out dramatically in the December and March positions, and I have to believe thay have taken protection and tried to build a little cushion to go through the frost season."

Frost can dramatically reduce the crop in Brazil, the number one coffee exporter, if it occurs in May or June as Brazil's coffee is maturing. Worries about the Brazilian crop and lower supplies from Colombia and Central America doubled coffee prices between December and March this year.

On Wednesday, traders' nerves continued to be jolted by the labor news out of South America. A strike by stevedores at Brazil's leading coffee port, Santos, was set to spread nationally on Friday. In Colombia, the number two coffee exporter, a truckers' strike was set to start on Sunday, April 20.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices fell sharply as a leading oil industry trade group said gasoline supplies were sufficient to meet even the most aggressive demand this spring and summer.
Gasoline for May delivery ended 1.52 cents a gallon lower at 60.38 cents, with May crude oil ending down 48 cents a barrel at $19.35 and May heating oil down 1.37 cents a gallon at 53.48 cents.

On Wednesday, the American Petroleum Institute said in its annual outlook for the summer peak driving season that U.S. gasoline supplies should be sufficient to accommodate a 2.5 percent growth rate in demand, the upper range of estimates.
The outlook followed its weekly oil inventory data released Tuesday evening which said gasoline stocks swelled 3.63 million barrels. Traders had expected a decline of 1 million to 2 million barrels.
"The data was a surprise because people were looking for seasonal demand for gasoline and they are not getting it, which is a disappointment," said Victor Yu, vice president of Refco Inc.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, cattle prices were jolted by panic selling when word circulated of reports of the death of an Indiana man from Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), a degenerative condition known as the human version of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
BSE is the "mad cow disease" that triggered a worldwide panic about beef consumption when a new strain of CJD in Britain last year was linked to the cattle disease.
BSE was first reported in British cattle in 1986.

Indiana health officials said several cases of CJD have occurred since 1990 in the state, but none have ever been linked to BSE. About 200 people a year die of CJD in the United States but no case of BSE has ever been detected in the country, the Centers for Disease Control in Atlanta said.
But the report still sparked a storm of nervous selling.
April live cattle futures closed at 68.80 cents a pound, down the 1.50 cent daily limit allowed by the exchange.

"Until there is some evidence that bovine spongiform encephalopathy...is present in the U.S. cattle population, I think there there is no reason for futures react to those kinds of stories," said analyst Chuck Levitt of Alaron Trading Corp.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, nervous selling tied to the BSE story also helped pushed down the price of corn, the main ingredient in cattle feed, traders said.
Corn for May delivery closed down 5-1/2 cents a bushel at $2.97-1/4.
